stoicism: If the deployment was judged with care on the evidence there was, the lack of an explanation takes nothing from its soundness.
What was in the deployers' power was the judgement to deploy; whether the people decided about can follow its reasons was never part of that.
An explanation would be welcome, yet nothing in the decision's soundness waits on it; only the weighing of the evidence does.
Look at how the people who chose to run it reasoned, and the silence of the system becomes a lesser matter.
utilitarianism: Every month the system waits for an explanation nobody can give is a month of suffering it could have prevented.
Set the unease of an unexplained decision beside the pain the system removes, and the second is far heavier.
Holding back a remedy that works, for want of a reason it can give, puts a principle above the people who are hurting.
If the benefit is as reliable as the motion says, those it reaches are better off with it than without it, told or not.
virtue-ethics: A just institution owes everyone it rules on an account, and a good outcome does not discharge that debt.
Deploying what nobody can explain trains its keepers out of the habit of answering for what they do.
The fair official explains a decision even when it is kind, because being owed reasons is part of being treated as a person.
Relief that arrives without reasons may be welcome, but accepting it as normal would make us careless about justice.
confucian: Whoever decides about a person owes that person an account, and a benefit that cannot be accounted for leaves the relationship unpaid.
Doing good that no one can question is not yet governing well, because governing well includes being answerable to the governed.
Let the system wait until those who run it can say why it decides as it does, and the people it serves can hold them to that.
Good done through a hidden mechanism teaches nobody how to do good, and that is a loss the relief does not repay.
ubuntu: People spared harm by a system they had no say in are still left outside the decision, and that exclusion is itself a harm.
Bring those it decides about into the deciding first; a benefit worth having will survive the wait.
Relief handed down without reasons treats the people it reaches as recipients rather than as members of a shared life.
The test is whether the families and neighbours affected could question the system together, and as it stands they cannot.
buddhist: Run it, but keep asking whom it still harms, since sparing suffering in most cases does not excuse the harm it does in the rest.
The intention to relieve suffering is good, and it stays good only while those running the system keep watching what it does.
A benefit no one can explain has to be watched all the more closely, because no one can see in advance where it will go wrong.
Compassion here means deploying it and then attending, case by case, to the people it decides about, told why or not.

stoicism: Publish the rule before anyone steps in, and the passenger who accepts it has judged for themselves what the car may do.
The deaths in the crash are not in anyone's power; whether the rule was disclosed and freely accepted is.
A passenger kept ignorant of the rule has been denied the one thing that was theirs here, an informed assent.
Which rule the car follows matters less than whether every passenger could look at it beforehand and agree.
utilitarianism: One death is fewer than two, and a car built to choose the lesser loss saves lives in every crash it cannot avoid.
Give the passenger and the pedestrians equal weight, and the arithmetic leaves only one programme to write.
A car that protects its owner at the cost of more lives is selling safety to one person by spending it on others.
Across millions of journeys, minimising deaths is the rule under which each traveller, passenger or not, is likeliest to live.
virtue-ethics: Wisdom here lies in how carefully the choice was weighed by the people who made it, not in whether their rule wins a count.
Any programmed rule can be prudent or reckless, and only the judgement of the people who set it can make it wise.
Treating the crash as a sum lets the builders feel they have decided well without ever having weighed the case.
The car will do what it was told, so the virtue that counts is in the telling, in how honestly and carefully the makers chose.
confucian: The maker took on a duty to the person riding in the car, and a count of strangers does not cancel what was promised.
Before asking how many die, ask what each party owed the others when the passenger got in, and who answers if that is broken.
Counting the passenger as one unit among many forgets the relationship that put them in the car's care.
Name the duties correctly, the maker's to the passenger and the driver's to the street, and the rule has to honour both.
ubuntu: The rule should be one that passengers and the people on the street could agree on together, not a sum worked out for them.
Who is in this crash is a matter of people sharing a road, and they, not a formula, should settle what the car does.
A rule nobody affected was asked about treats passengers and walkers as numbers, whatever number it saves.
Ask whether walkers and riders were ever drawn into writing the rule, and today the honest answer is no.
buddhist: Whoever writes the rule forms an intention about who will die, and that intention should be the one compassion would choose.
Impartial compassion does not rank the passenger above the child crossing, so fewer deaths is the intention to build in.
The makers cannot hand this choice to the car; whatever it does in the crash was willed by them long before.
Building in the smallest loss is right only if the makers keep owning that choice and keep looking at whom the rule still harms.

stoicism: Without a ruling faculty to give or withhold assent, the model produces outputs, and calling them decisions borrows a word it cannot earn.
Assent belongs to whoever reads the output and acts on it, and that is where the deciding happens.
Keep the word for beings that judge their impressions, and the motion is plainly right.
A model can be well made or badly made, but it cannot decide, because nothing in it is in its own power.
utilitarianism: Call it deciding or not, the output reaches the same people with the same effects, and those effects are what need weighing.
The argument over the word would matter only if changing it changed the harm, and it does not.
Spend the effort on what the model's outputs do to people, because renaming them changes no one's life.
Whether anything decided inside the system is a question with no victims either way; the outputs are where the welfare is.
virtue-ethics: Only a settled character can choose well or badly, and the model has a training history where a character would be.
Deliberation belongs to someone who could have wanted otherwise, and nothing in the model wants anything.
Keep decision for creatures who can be praised or blamed for their choices, and the model plainly falls outside it.
To say the model decided is to excuse the people whose deliberation, good or bad, stands behind each output.
confucian: Correct naming is the start of correct conduct, and here it points every question back to the office that deployed the model.
If the word decide drifts to the machine, the official who relied on it will soon believe nothing was theirs to answer for.
Rectify the name and the question of who must answer becomes simple again: the person whose office it was.
A decision is something a person in a role owes others, and the model holds no role to owe it from.
ubuntu: Credit the machine with the choice and those affected are left with nobody to answer them.
Deciding happens among people who answer to one another, and the model answers to no one.
Reserve the word for people, so that those touched by the output can still find who decided and ask why.
The word also buries a second question, which voices were never heard when the system was set to work.
buddhist: Where there is no volition there is no deciding, only a result arising from conditions the deployers set.
The intention lies with those who trained and deployed the model, so that is where the moral weight of each output rests.
Naming an output a decision invents an agent and lets the real intentions go unexamined.
Look for the will behind the act and it is found in the people who built and used the system, never in the model.

stoicism: A trained model can be a fine instrument, but an instrument assents to nothing, and so it can be neither virtuous nor vicious.
Feedback shapes behaviour from outside, while goodness in a person is learned by judging their own impressions.
The model's outputs may help or harm, and like every external they carry no virtue of their own.
Upbringing aims at a mind that can judge for itself; training aims at outputs, and that is a different end.
utilitarianism: If the trained model reliably does more good than harm, calling it good says everything that needs saying.
Upbringing matters in people for what it leads them to do, and judged by what it leads to, training can match it.
Ask what the trained behaviour does for the people it serves; the inner life it lacks changes none of those results.
A view that counts only consequences has no reason to care whether goodness arrived by upbringing or by feedback.
virtue-ethics: Habituation succeeds when the habit becomes a settled choice of one's own, a stage reward shaping never reaches.
The trained model performs the acts of a good person without the character that would make them virtuous.
Moral upbringing aims at someone who does the right thing for its own sake; training aims at the right output, which is less.
Good acts without a good character are imitation, however reliable, and imitation is not what upbringing produces.
confucian: A child is raised into a household's ways over years; the model is raised into nothing, only scored.
Humaneness is learned from parents, teachers and elders over years, and no score stands in for that slow education.
A model may learn to say the right words, but it has no role in which to practise them and no elder or child to practise them for.
Ritual shapes the heart as well as the act, and feedback shapes only what the model returns.
ubuntu: Raters can reward a reply, but nobody can draw a model into a family, and that drawing in is how goodness grows.
Goodness grows through the people around us, and the model has raters, not relationships.
Feedback can teach a system what pleases, but becoming good is something people do together over a shared life.
Training adjusts outputs one score at a time, while upbringing makes someone a member of a community, and that is the difference.
buddhist: Training hands the model effects without any will behind them, and goodness asks for the will as much as the effects.
A model that has learned to say kind things has not formed the volition that makes kindness good.
A good upbringing trains attention over a lifetime; feedback trains only what comes out.
The harm the trained model avoids is welcome, but goodness in the sense of upbringing needs a will to train, and there is none.

stoicism: Fortune decided the size of the harm; the builders' judgement is the only thing blame can fairly attach to.
Bad luck can multiply the damage without adding anything to the fault, because the fault lay only in the judging.
Measure blame by the care in the judging, not by the outcome, which was never in the builder's power.
Proportion to the harm would blame people for what happened to them rather than for what they did.
utilitarianism: Blame is worth assigning only where it changes future behaviour, and punishing careful builders changes nothing for the better.
Proportional blame would teach builders that care does not pay, and less care means more harm next time.
Aim blame where it can change what happens next, and the careful builder is the wrong target.
The useful question is which incentives reduce future harm, and blaming bad luck is not one of them.
virtue-ethics: A good builder will grieve the harm and work to repair it, but grief owed is a different thing from blame earned.
Proportional blame confuses regret, which the careful builder rightly feels, with fault, which they do not bear.
The builder who shrugs at the harm shows a flaw of character; the one who was careful and grieves does not.
Judge the builder by how they built and how they respond, and the size of the damage is not the measure.
confucian: A role's debts are fixed by the role, not by fortune, and a builder who paid them in full is not in default.
If the builders did what their position required, the harm alone cannot make them guilty.
Duty done is duty done; what remains is the duty to set things right for those who were harmed.
What remains owed after the harm is an explanation and help for those injured, which differs from owing blame sized to the injury.
ubuntu: The harm asks the makers to come back to those it fell on and help set things right, which no amount of blame achieves.
Careful builders still owe the injured their presence and their help, because the harm broke a relationship they share.
A verdict of guilt closes a file, but restoring the people harmed to the life they share with others is the work that matters.
Ask what would mend things between the makers and those hurt, and the answer is repair, not a measure of guilt.
buddhist: An act made with care and good will is judged by that will as well, so measuring blame by the damage alone misjudges it.
The harm still calls on the builders to attend to those it hurt, but attending is not the same as being to blame.
Blame that ignores volition judges an act by half of what makes it what it is.
Judge such builders by what they intended, and then ask them to keep watching what the system does to people.

stoicism: Your own reason is the one thing truly yours, and no better outcome repays handing it away.
Better choices made for you are still made for you, and the use of your own reason is what was lost.
Every choice handed over is a judgement not exercised, and the faculty weakens with each one.
Outcomes were never yours to secure; your own judging was, and that is exactly what the assistant takes.
utilitarianism: A happier life with better decisions in it has lost nothing that matters, whoever made them.
A life that goes better by every measure you care about cannot be worse because someone else did the choosing.
Caring who did the choosing is a kind of pride, and pride counts for little beside days that go better.
Count what you gain in time and good outcomes against what you lose, and the loss is hard to find.
virtue-ethics: Wisdom grows only by use, so someone who delegates every choice stays as unwise as the day they began.
An assistant's better choices leave you with good outcomes and no practice in choosing well.
Character is built from small decisions made daily, and handing those over hands over the building.
A person who never chooses never becomes anyone in particular, however well their days go.
confucian: Every role is learned by doing what it asks, and a role done by proxy is not learned at all.
A child whose gifts for a grandparent are chosen by an assistant has given something, but has not yet learned to give.
Conduct grows through practice inside one's relationships, so outsourcing the practice leaves the relationships thinner.
Better choices bought at the price of never practising one's roles are a poor exchange.
ubuntu: A person is made in the choices shared with others, and no assistant can do that making for anyone.
When the assistant chooses the gift or the reply, the person loses an exchange through which they belong to others.
Better choices that no longer pass between people cost the very relationships that made them worth making.
What matters is not whether the choice is better but whether it is still made together, and handing it over ends that.
buddhist: Nothing permanent is lost, yet each choice handed over is one less occasion to notice what is intended and who is hurt.
What suffers is not an owner of choices but the practice of noticing, choice by choice, what one intends and whom it hurts.
A better choice made without attention trains no compassion, and attention is what each daily choice could have trained.
Hand over what you will, but keep watching the intention behind each choice, since that watching is the practice that matters.
